result.summary: Apollo is shown playing his lyre among the delighted gods on Olympus. The poet then follows Apollo's journey across Greece in search of a site for his oracle, until Telphusa tricks him into choosing Crisa below Parnassus.

scenes.title: Apollo's lyre on Olympus
scenes.summary: Apollo goes from Pytho to Olympus and plays the lyre while the Muses sing and the other gods dance.

scenes.title: Apollo searches for an oracle site
scenes.summary: The poet recalls Apollo's wooing and then his journey through Pieria, Euboea and Boeotia seeking a place for an oracle.

scenes.title: Onchestus and the Cephissus
scenes.summary: Apollo passes Poseidon's grove at Onchestus, where chariot-dedication rites are described, then crosses the Cephissus to Haliartus.

scenes.title: Telphusa redirects Apollo
scenes.summary: Apollo plans a temple at Telphusa's spring. She warns of horse noise and persuades him to build at Crisa instead.
scenes.stakes: Telphusa wants the renown of the oracle for herself; Apollo risks a poor site for his temple.

scenes.title: Arrival at Crisa
scenes.summary: Apollo passes the Phlegyae and reaches Crisa beneath Parnassus, where he resolves to build his temple.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Hermes, who killed the watcher Argus; not named directly here.
Cult title 'Hail-Healer' that Telphusa says men will give Apollo.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable picture of gods delighting in song while mortals suffer, helpless against death and old age.

analysis.text: The passage contrasts Apollo's serene divine music with human frailty, then turns to his founding of the oracle at Delphi.
The tale of Telphusa explains the origin of Delphi and reflects the geography and cult sites of Boeotia and Phocis.

fun_facts.text: Line 8 has a gap in the manuscripts, so the list of Apollo's wooings is incomplete.

language_notes.text: Lycia, Maeonia (Lydia) and Miletus are regions and a city in Asia Minor where Apollo was widely worshipped; Delos was his birthplace.
The 'golden key' is the plectrum, the pick used to strike the lyre's strings.
'Witless and helpless' describes humans, who live without understanding and cannot cure death or escape old age.
'Featly' means neatly and nimbly, describing Apollo's graceful stepping.
'Slayer of Argus' is Hermes, who killed the hundred-eyed giant Argus.
A list of Apollo's legendary love pursuits; the text is damaged here, and a lacuna (gap) interrupts it.
The Euripus is the narrow strait between Euboea and the Boeotian mainland.
The horses rattle the empty chariot freely; if it breaks, the men tend the horses but tilt the broken chariot against something and leave it to the god.
Hecatombs were large public sacrifices, originally of a hundred oxen, here meaning splendid offerings generally.
'Do you lay up my words in your heart' means 'store them in your mind and remember them'.
Iepaeon, glossed as 'Hail-Healer', is a cult title of Apollo from the cry 'Ie Paean', linking him to healing and paeans.
The translation uses 'Zeus' here, though elsewhere this edition may differ; the Phlegyae are described as showing contempt for the god.

context_notes.text: The Graces, Seasons, Harmonia and Hebe are minor goddesses of beauty, the year, concord and youth, often shown dancing with the Olympians.
The poet turns to Apollo's founding of his oracle, which leads to Delphi (Pytho).
Thebe stands empty because the city of Thebes had not yet been founded in this mythic time.
Onchestus in Boeotia had a grove sacred to Poseidon, who was closely connected with horses.
Telphusa is a nymph of a spring, here the local spirit of a site Apollo wants for his oracle.
Crisa lies below Parnassus near Delphi; Apollo's temple here becomes the Delphic oracle.

literary_notes.text: The gods' joyful music is set against the Muses' song of human suffering, underscoring the gap between mortal and immortal life.
'Who delights in arrows' characterizes Artemis by her hunting nature while praising her stature and beauty.
The poet's questions about what to sing serve as a transition, offering the next themes of the hymn.
Green hills, grassy beds and wheat-bearing plains evoke an untouched landscape before human settlement.
The narrator addresses Apollo directly, 'O worker from afar', giving the journey a hymnic, ritual tone.
Telphusa flatters Apollo's strength while steering him away, showing her as cunning and deferential.
Telphusa's selfish motive is exposed, yet her trick fails to benefit her; she only removes Apollo from her spring, foreshadowing later punishment.
